newsitem.title: GERMANY: Leading German banker sees leeway on EMU criteria.
newsitem.headline: Leading German banker sees leeway on EMU criteria.

text.p: Commerzbank AG chief executive Martin Kohlhaussen, newly-appointed head of Germany's top banking federation, said there was room for interpretation in the criteria for Europe's monetary union.
"Neither the deficit criterion or the debt quotient has to be met exactly on the spot," Kohlhaussen said in an interview with Reuters.
The Commerzbank chief cautioned that any leeway on the Maastricht Treaty criteria could be used "only in narrow margins, and responsibly."
But he said he had no reason to doubt that Germany would make the grade to take part in monetary union from the start.

To qualify for Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), national budget deficits must not exceed three percent of GDP and debt levels must not exceed 60 percent of GDP, according to the Maastricht Treaty.

However the treaty also leaves some scope for manouevre around these numerical thresholds -- an issue which has become a hot topic as concerns mount that Germany will struggle to meet Maastricht demands this year, as it must in order to take part in the scheduled euro launch in January 1999.

Kohlhaussen, who was this month elected president of the Federation of German Banks, also said that while the German public was still mainly sceptical about the euro, more and more people had come to expect currency union to start on time.
"It is now crucial to make clearer to the public the economic advantages of a stable euro and work decisively toward fulfilling the convergence criteria in accordance with the treaty," he said.
Kohlhaussen said the switch to a common currency would sharpen competition in Europe but also offered enormous chances for an export-driven country like Germany.
"In order to use these, urgent reforms are needed. Here I am thinking principally of tax reform and reform of our social security system," Kohlhaussen said.
Banks had led the way in adjusting their operations for the euro launch but Kohlhaussen said banks had noted an increasing willingness to prepare from other firms as well.
"The realisation is also growing in other sectors that any delay in preparations will send costs rocketing," he said.
